query: Which method can be used for oxidation resistance, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Applying first-principles density functional theory (DFT) calculations to screen and predict alloy compositions will enable the design of metal/alloy surfaces that form stable and protective oxide layers, thereby enhancing oxidation resistance under high-temperature conditions.
generation.material_initial_state: Metal or alloy surfaces (e.g., high-entropy or refractory alloys) that are inherently susceptible to oxidation in high-temperature or oxidative environments.
generation.intervention: Use DFT-based computational screening to evaluate the energy barriers and stability of potential oxide phases on various alloy compositions.
generation.conditions: High-temperature oxidation or corrosive atmospheric conditions where oxide layer formation governs material degradation.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of coherent, dense, and low-energy oxide scales on the alloy surface, as predicted by DFT calculations.
generation.mechanism: Stable oxide layers act as passivating barriers that slow oxygen diffusion and prevent further oxidation; DFT identifies alloy compositions that promote the formation of such protective scales, thereby reducing overall oxidation kinetics.
generation.predicted_outcome: Alloys selected based on DFT predictions will exhibit significantly reduced oxidation rates compared to baseline alloys, due to the formation of more stable and protective oxide scales.
generation.baseline: Conventional alloy compositions developed without DFT-guided optimization, which typically display higher oxidation rates and less protective oxide scales.
generation.boundary: The effectiveness of this approach is expected to be most pronounced in high-temperature regimes; its applicability to lower temperature or less oxidative environments remains to be verified.
generation.uncertainty: While DFT predictions can indicate potential improvements in oxide stability, experimental uncertainties and scale-mechanism complexities (such as stress-induced spallation or competing oxide phase formation) may impact the observed oxidation resistance.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of alloys: one group designed via DFT screening for stable, low-energy oxide layer formation and a control group designed without such computational guidance. Subject both groups to identical high-temperature oxidation tests.
measurements: Mass gain over time to assess oxidation kinetics
Phase identification and integrity of the oxide scale via X-ray diffraction (XRD)
Surface morphology and cross-sectional analysis using electron microscopy
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the DFT-designed alloys do not show at least a 20% reduction in oxidation rate or improved oxide scale integrity relative to the control group under the same high-temperature conditions, the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
First reported in 2004 [ [1] ], high-entropy alloys (HEAs) are alloys comprising five or more elements in equal or nearly equal molar fractions, with each element present at a mole fraction of approximately 5–35 at.% [ [2] ]. The presence of multiple elements leads to a high configurational entropy, resulting in solid-solution structures with face-centred cubic (FCC) and body-centred cubic (BCC) lattices, rather than intermetallic compounds [ [3] ]. In recent years, HEAs have garnered significant consideration in the field of materials science because of their exceptional performance characteristics, including high strength [ [4] ], corrosion resistance [ [5] ], soft magnetic properties [ [6] ], high hardness [ [7] ], wear resistance [ [8] ], fatigue resistance [ [9] ], and softening resistance at high temperatures [ [10] ]. The superior high-temperature behaviour of HEAs can be attributed to four underlying effects: the high entropy effect, the sluggish kinetic diffusion effect, the severe lattice distortion effect, and the cocktail effect [ [11] ].
